explanation: Digital Workflow Leadership is the capability to lead the selection, deployment, and governance of enterprise digital platforms that support needs identification, workflow design, and workflow configuration. It includes using business intelligence, metadata-driven tools, automation, and AI-enabled triage to create standardized, auditable, and reusable processes that reduce manual handoffs and support scalable, interoperable operations.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires a shift from manual, expert-driven planning to digitally enabled, enterprise-wide needs identification and workflow orchestration. The change drivers directly influence activities 1.1, 2.6, and 3.4 by requiring staff to use standardized discovery platforms, embed automation and machine-actionable metadata early, and lead modular, version-controlled, self-service workflow environments aligned with enterprise governance and strategic priorities.

explanation: Business Intelligence & Analytics is the capability to use business intelligence tools, dashboards, metadata platforms, and analytical methods to identify needs, assess options, and prioritize work based on cost, impact, reuse, and strategic fit. In practice, this supports more digital and evidence-based needs identification, stronger stakeholder consultations using existing data assets, and action plans that can be tracked transparently through integrated dashboards and automated workflows.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to more digital, integrated, and data-driven decision making, with greater use of automation and AI in planning and delivery. Those change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 8.3 by requiring staff to use business intelligence and metadata tools to triage requests, confirm needs against existing assets, apply cost-benefit and prioritization criteria, and monitor action plans through transparent, dashboard-enabled governance.

explanation: Automation & Process Re-engineering is the capability to redesign statistical work so teams first use automated, reusable, and digitally enabled solutions before considering new surveys or manual processes. It includes assessing existing data sources, configuring modular collection or extraction tools, and operating automated workflows with staff focused more on monitoring, exception handling, interoperability, and auditability than on manual collection tasks.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point to an automation-first, cost-conscious, and digitally integrated operating model. These drivers reshape future work in GSBPM 1.1, 3.1, and 4.3 by requiring staff to triage needs against existing data and reusable solutions, build or adapt metadata-driven automated instruments, and run collection through automated pipelines with minimal manual intervention.

explanation: This capability is the ability to use digital triage tools and structured justification frameworks to assess new or modified statistical program requests before launching new collection. It supports identifying needs, checking data availability and suitability, and preparing business cases by systematically comparing existing data, administrative or alternative sources, automation opportunities, and survey options using cost, risk, impact, reusability, and strategic fit criteria.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to more digitally enabled, enterprise-wide decision-making, stronger use of existing and alternative data, and greater emphasis on automation, efficiency, and transparent prioritization. These change drivers directly influence GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 1.6 by requiring staff to use automated discovery and triage tools, document why new surveys are necessary, and build evidence-based business cases that prioritize reuse, sustainability, and alignment with enterprise platforms.

explanation: Data Asset Inventory & Governance is the capability to systematically identify, catalogue, assess, and steward internal and external data assets using standardized metadata, governance rules, and reusable digital tools. It enables staff to quickly determine what data already exists, whether it is suitable for use, and how it can be integrated, reused, and governed before proposing new collection. This supports more automated, auditable, and enterprise-wide decision-making across needs identification, data availability assessment, and data integration.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires Statistics Canada to prioritize reuse of existing data, strengthen enterprise data stewardship, and reduce unnecessary new collection through digital-first, evidence-based processes. The change drivers directly influence GSBPM activities 1.1, 1.5, and 5.1 by requiring automated data discovery, machine-actionable metadata, formal justification for new surveys, and interoperable integration practices. As a result, employees need stronger capability in data inventory management and governance frameworks to support transparent, scalable, and compliant use of data assets.

explanation: Digital Change Management is the capability to lead teams through digital transformation by embedding automation, data asset thinking, and continuous upskilling into day-to-day management. In practice, this means Chiefs must help staff shift from manual, survey-first approaches to digitally enabled ways of working across needs identification, workflow design, and dissemination, while building confidence with standardized tools, reusable systems, and governed release platforms.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to a future operating model centered on modernization, automation, reuse of data assets, and digitally enabled service delivery. These change drivers directly influence future work requirements in activities such as identifying needs through enterprise data scanning, designing modular automated workflows, and managing governed dissemination platforms, making Chief-led change management and workforce upskilling essential to avoid lagging in adoption and performance.

explanation: Platform-driven Asset Evaluation is the capability to use digital discovery and metadata platforms to systematically identify, assess, and compare existing statistical assets before proposing new collection or program development. It supports faster, evidence-based needs identification and consultation by enabling automated suitability screening, transparent reuse analysis, and iterative planning grounded in what data already exists and how well it meets emerging requirements.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 shifts staff toward platform-enabled identification of needs, consultation, and automated assessment of data availability and suitability, with new surveys becoming exceptions that require strong evidence. This direction is driven by Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which emphasize reuse of existing data, digital platforms, automation, transparency, and more agile, strategic decision-making—thereby making platform analysis and digital asset catalogue expertise essential for future work.

explanation: Automated Asset Review is the capability to use enterprise platforms, metadata, and automated screening tools to quickly assess whether existing internal, administrative, or alternative data assets can meet a business need before proposing new collection. It includes documenting reuse decisions, suitability findings, validation considerations, and cost-benefit evidence in a transparent, auditable way, while reserving human judgment for complex, high-risk, or novel cases.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a shift toward reuse-first, digitally enabled, and transparent statistical production, where new surveys must be justified as exceptions rather than defaults. That direction directly changes future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 5.3 by requiring staff to use automated discovery and consultation tools, assess data availability and suitability systematically, and support standardized, auditable review and validation processes that inform faster, evidence-based decisions.

explanation: This capability is the ability to build and document a clear business case for new surveys by comparing costs, benefits, risks, and expected outcomes against existing internal, administrative, and alternative data sources. In future needs identification, consultation, and data availability assessment, staff must use digital discovery platforms, metadata, and standardized decision tools to show why a new survey is necessary, reusable, strategically aligned, and worth the investment.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a shift toward reuse of existing data, digital-first decision making, transparency, and more efficient, sustainable statistical production. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 by requiring staff to conduct platform-based asset reviews, assess feasibility and trade-offs, and provide rigorous evidence before any new survey proceeds.

explanation: Agile, platform-supported prioritization is the capability to use digital platforms, metadata tools, and structured decision processes to continuously assess needs, compare options, and update priorities as new evidence emerges. It enables staff to integrate cross-functional input, evaluate reuse of existing data before proposing new collection, and manage faster review cycles with transparent decision logging across needs identification, consultation, and dissemination planning.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to more digitally enabled, enterprise-wide prioritization, stronger reuse of existing data assets, and faster iterative decision-making. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 3.3, these change drivers increase the need for employees to use platform-enabled tools to assess feasibility, cost-benefit, strategic fit, interoperability, and reuse, directly shaping future work toward agile, evidence-based prioritization rather than isolated program-level decisions.

explanation: This capability is the ability to engage clients quickly and transparently using digital consultation, metadata, and asset platforms to confirm needs, assess reuse options, and support clear trade-off discussions. It includes navigating searchable data assets, facilitating agile consultation cycles, and using standardized platform tools to document decisions, improve transparency, and connect stakeholder input to reusable dissemination and release processes.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to more open, digital, reusable, and platform-based ways of working, which directly changes how needs are consulted, solutions are built, and products are released. These drivers increase the need for employees to use machine-actionable metadata, standardized dissemination platforms, and auditable workflows to support faster consultation, stronger reuse decisions, and transparent client engagement aligned with feasibility, timeliness, and enterprise priorities.

explanation: Evidence-Based Negotiation is the capability to negotiate resources, services, and delivery timelines using platform-supported evidence, searchable metadata, and transparent cost-benefit analysis rather than relying primarily on precedent or informal judgment. In practice, it enables employees to guide stakeholder discussions on asset reuse, feasibility, value, and trade-offs, while documenting decisions and action plans through dashboards and standardized workflows. This capability is especially important in needs consultation, data availability assessment, and action planning, where negotiations must be faster, more transparent, and tied to measurable outcomes.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to more digital, transparent, and efficiency-driven decision-making, where new work must be justified against existing assets and strategic priorities. The change drivers indicate that consultations, data source assessments, and action plans will increasingly rely on machine-actionable metadata, automated suitability screening, and platform-based tracking, which raises the need for staff who can negotiate using evidence, explain trade-offs clearly, and justify resource requests with rigorous outcome-focused analysis. As a result, negotiation is no longer only relationship-based; it is directly shaped by these change drivers into a more structured, evidence-led capability required for future operations.

explanation: Cross-Functional Integration is the capability to coordinate evaluation and program activities across sectors using shared digital platforms, interoperable tools, and reusable assets. It includes configuring and validating integration rules, using dashboards and metadata to support continuous evaluation, and working with business, IT, and program teams in agile cycles to improve processes and extend existing solutions rather than building new ones from scratch.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively emphasize greater horizontal collaboration, digital enablement, reuse of existing assets, and faster integrated delivery across the organization. These drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 5.1, 8.2, and 1.2 by requiring employees to operate within interoperable platforms, support real-time evaluation and exception management, and lead cross-sector consultation using metadata-driven tools and agile decision processes.

explanation: Automation and Digital Workflow Integration is the capability to design statistical programs so automation, reusable digital workflows, and machine-actionable outputs are built in from the start. It requires assessing automation readiness, workflow interoperability, metadata-driven design, and opportunities for modular reuse across needs identification, processing and analysis, and production system design so programs are auditable, scalable, and less dependent on manual intervention.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a shift toward modernized, digitally enabled, efficient, and reusable statistical operations. Those change drivers directly influence future work requirements in GSBPM 1.1, 2.5, and 2.6 by requiring feasibility assessments for automation and reuse, machine-actionable and metadata-driven design, and interoperable production workflows, making advanced capability in automation and digital workflow integration essential for strategy formation.

skill_gap: Cost/Benefit Analysis for Automation vs. Survey Approaches
explanation: This capability is the ability to systematically compare traditional survey approaches with automated, digital, administrative, or reusable data options by assessing cost, effort, timeliness, quality, risk, and scalability. It supports early needs identification, data availability assessment, and business case development by ensuring staff can determine when a survey is truly necessary and when a more automated, enterprise-aligned solution is the better choice.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 1.6 requires staff to justify new collection through structured cost-benefit, feasibility, and trade-off analysis before proceeding to survey design. This is directly driven by Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize digital-first service delivery, automation readiness, reuse of existing assets and data sources, and transparent, evidence-based decisions aligned to enterprise priorities.

skill_gap: Automation Frameworks and Digital Asset Evaluation
explanation: This capability is the ability to assess automation frameworks, reusable digital assets, and interoperability requirements so that program designs and recommendations are standardized, modular, and ready for automated workflows. It supports work in identifying needs, designing processing and analysis, and designing production systems by ensuring solutions are metadata-driven, auditable, reusable, and compatible with cross-program digital platforms from the outset.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change to work requires recommendations to be assessed against automation readiness, asset reuse, and digital workflow compatibility before approval, directly increasing expectations in GSBPM 1.1, 2.5, and 2.6. It is driven by the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize digital-first modernization, interoperability, reuse of enterprise assets, automation, and scalable workflow design, thereby shaping future work toward modular, machine-actionable, and enterprise-aligned solutions.

explanation: Digital interoperability and machine-actionability is the capability to evaluate whether systems, data sources, and processing designs can work seamlessly within a digital-first statistical ecosystem using standardized metadata, FAIR principles, and reusable, automated workflows. It enables the Chief to ensure new technologies support automated data discovery, integration, and processing across activities such as checking data suitability, integrating data, and designing processing and analysis, while reserving human effort for exceptions, risk assessment, and partner management.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires automated data discovery, interoperable integration architectures, and machine-actionable, metadata-driven processing designs across GSBPM 1.5, 5.1, and 2.5. It is also reinforced by Mandate letter expectations for modern, digital-first, efficient government services, which means the Chief must be able to assess whether new systems, data sources, and technologies meet interoperability and automation requirements before they are adopted.

explanation: Digital Evaluation Framework Development is the capability to design and use structured criteria that assess whether statistical programs, methods, and assets are ready for automation, interoperable with digital workflows, and suitable for reuse. It supports earlier, more systematic decision-making at needs identification, design, and evaluation stages by embedding standardized measures, dashboard-ready indicators, and FAIR-aligned considerations into program review and approval processes.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a shift toward digital-first, automated, interoperable, and reusable statistical operations. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 2.5, and 8.2 by requiring explicit assessment of automation readiness, modular reuse, continuous monitoring, and system-generated evaluation data, making new evaluation frameworks essential for planning, design, and real-time oversight.

skill_gap: Digital Change Management and Team Enablement
explanation: Digital Change Management and Team Enablement is the capability to lead teams through the adoption of automated, interoperable, and machine-actionable ways of working while ensuring staff can assess digital feasibility, redesign processes, and use standardized workflow tools effectively. It includes guiding training, knowledge transfer, and role clarity so multidisciplinary teams can design reusable, auditable, metadata-driven workflows and document needs in ways that support downstream automation and scalable production systems.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires leaders to move beyond traditional oversight and actively enable teams to deliver automation-ready, digitally integrated work. The change drivers point to greater use of standardized platforms, self-service workflow configuration, interoperability, and machine-actionable documentation across activities such as identifying needs, designing production systems, and configuring workflows, which directly increases the need for chiefs who can mentor staff, manage process change, and build team readiness for digital transformation.

explanation: AI & Machine Learning Contextualization is the capability to assess, validate, and apply AI-generated concepts, outputs, and frameworks so they remain statistically sound, program-relevant, and fit for operational use. As concept identification, interpretation, and editing/imputation become more automated, the role shifts from manual production to human oversight, exception handling, ethical review, and ensuring outputs align with metadata standards, FAIR principles, and end-to-end digital integration.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to greater automation, digital integration, trusted use of AI, and faster delivery of data products, which directly changes work in GSBPM 1.4, 5.4, and 6.3. These drivers increase the need for staff to validate machine-generated concepts and outputs, arbitrate exceptions, assess fairness and methodological limits, and ensure automated results are reusable, auditable, and aligned with standardized metadata and program needs.

explanation: Digital Integration & Strategic Arbitration is the capability to lead cross-team decisions in environments where AI and automated tools generate concepts, workflows, and analytical outputs. It involves validating machine-generated options, establishing reusable and interoperable digital integration frameworks, and resolving conflicts between automated recommendations, business priorities, and ethical or quality requirements. As work shifts from manual evaluation to oversight, this capability ensures automated pipelines remain trusted, aligned, and operationally effective.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to more integrated, automated, and AI-enabled operations that require stronger human oversight, cross-functional coordination, and decision arbitration. The future-state requirements in GSBPM 1.4, 2.5, and 6.3 show that concept identification, processing design, and output interpretation will increasingly rely on machine-generated suggestions, modular digital workflows, and metadata-driven tools, making it essential for the Chief to validate automated frameworks, guide integration across teams, and arbitrate exceptions where human judgment must prevail.

explanation: Metadata Architecture & Interoperability is the capability to design, apply, and govern standardized metadata so concepts, data sources, and integrated outputs can move reliably across automated systems and teams. As work shifts from manual review to AI-enabled discovery, suitability assessment, and data integration, staff must validate machine-generated structures, manage exceptions, and ensure FAIR, reusable, and interoperable metadata supports rapid, auditable workflows.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to greater automation, enterprise integration, and reuse of data and methods across the statistical production process. In GSBPM 1.4, 1.5, and 5.1, these change drivers increase the need for standardized, machine-actionable metadata to support automated concept identification, data discovery and suitability screening, and interoperable AI-enabled integration, making metadata architecture a foundational requirement for future work.

explanation: Exception Validation & Arbitration is the capability to oversee AI-enabled validation processes, assess whether automated rules and outputs are complete, accurate, auditable, and ethically sound, and intervene when complex exceptions arise. As validation and review activities in GSBPM 5.3, 6.2, and 6.3 become increasingly automated, staff must shift from manual checking to monitoring validation logic, interpreting flagged anomalies, and making strategic decisions when automated results require human judgment.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the shift described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to greater use of AI, automation, standardized validation, and trusted digital-by-design statistical operations. These change drivers increase the need for employees who can validate exceptions, arbitrate ambiguous or high-stakes cases, and ensure AI-supported outputs remain aligned with program objectives, transparency requirements, and final accountability for data quality.

explanation: This capability enables staff to assess, select, and implement AI-enabled and automated statistical processes in ways that are reliable, auditable, and fit for operational use. It supports future work where evaluation is continuous and dashboard-driven, processing and analysis are designed as modular and machine-actionable workflows, and data suitability assessments increasingly rely on automated discovery, metadata, and decision rules.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide point to a stronger requirement for digital transformation, automation, and responsible use of AI across statistical operations. These drivers influence future work by requiring real-time evaluation (GSBPM 8.2), automation-ready process design (GSBPM 2.5), and automated data suitability assessment (GSBPM 1.5), making the ability to evaluate AI systems and their long-term program impacts essential.

explanation: AI-Driven Statistical Methodologies is the capability to apply modern AI techniques alongside statistical theory to identify concepts, design frames and samples, and interpret automated outputs within digital, metadata-driven production environments. It enables employees to oversee AI-supported pipelines, validate methodological choices, explain results in context, and ensure outputs remain transparent, ethical, reusable, and fit for decision-making.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to more digital, automated, and AI-enabled statistical operations, requiring staff to work differently across concept development, sample design, and analytical interpretation. These change drivers increase the need for expertise that combines traditional statistical methods with AI-driven approaches so employees can guide automated pipelines, assess quality and fairness, apply FAIR and metadata standards, and provide trusted human oversight over faster, higher-volume production.

explanation: Digital Project Management & Team Arbitration is the capability to lead modular, metadata-driven digital projects across business, IT, data engineering, and AI-enabled teams while coordinating decisions, roles, and trade-offs across domains. It includes managing standardized workflows, automation logic, version-controlled delivery, and clear arbitration mechanisms so processing, production, and action-planning activities remain auditable, reusable, and responsive in real time.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to a future operating model built on digital integration, automation, interoperability, and responsible AI-enabled decision making. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 2.5, 2.6, and 8.3 by requiring leaders who can coordinate cross-domain teams, govern metadata-driven and modular workflows, and arbitrate priorities and accountability in agile, digitally monitored environments.

explanation: This capability is the ability to understand how metadata-driven platforms enable automated, reusable, and auditable statistical workflows, and to use that understanding to shape program strategy. It includes guiding the design and use of machine-actionable metadata, modular processing rules, automated suitability screening, and AI-enabled dissemination so systems are optimized for findability, interoperability, quality, and governance. For a Chief, this means leading strategy that shifts work from manual execution toward platform configuration, oversight of automation logic, and performance monitoring across data discovery, processing, analysis, and dissemination.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to a statistical operating model built on automation, FAIR data practices, reusable components, and metadata-enabled platforms, while Mandate letters reinforce expectations for modern, digital, efficient, and responsive public service delivery. These change drivers directly influence future requirements in activities such as checking data availability and suitability, designing processing and analysis, and promoting dissemination products, where success depends on leaders being able to strategically adopt, validate, and optimize metadata-driven automated systems—capability not fully reflected in the current role description.

explanation: Automated decision logic validation is the capability to understand, test, and verify how metadata-driven rules, automated validation modules, and AI-supported decision processes produce results. In practice, it enables chiefs to oversee automated review and output validation processes, interpret exceptions, and ensure that validation logic is auditable, reproducible, legally compliant, and ethically sound across processing and analysis workflows.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to a shift toward automated, AI-enabled, metadata-driven, and auditable business processes, which changes chiefs’ roles from manual review to oversight of system logic and automated outputs. That direction directly influences future work in GSBPM 2.5, 5.3, and 6.2, where staff must design machine-actionable validation rules, monitor automated pipelines, validate exceptions, and assess legal, cost, transparency, and ethical implications of automated decisions.

explanation: This capability is the ability to interpret, validate, and act on outputs from automated suitability screening, metadata-driven discovery tools, and AI-enabled analytical workflows. It requires leaders to apply judgment to explain results in context, assess quality, fairness, legal and ethical risks, and use automated findings to support decisions, partnerships, and program actions. As work shifts from manual assessment toward human oversight of automated pipelines, this capability becomes essential for ensuring trust, relevance, and responsible use of system-generated evidence.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to increasing reliance on automated data discovery, AI-generated outputs, metadata-driven decision rules, and reusable automated processing designs across activities 1.5, 2.5, and 6.3. These change drivers mean Chiefs must move beyond traditional review roles to interpret automated suitability results, oversee ethical and methodological limits, and manage legal, privacy, and partnership risks arising from automated findings. The Mandate letters further reinforce expectations for transparent, responsible, and evidence-based decision-making, making this capability necessary even though it is not explicit in the current role description.

skill_gap: Legal/ethical risk management in data partnerships
explanation: This capability is the ability to assess and manage legal, privacy, and ethical risks when using alternative data partnerships, automated suitability screening, and automated decision outputs in statistical operations. It includes interpreting machine-generated recommendations, applying appropriate governance and disclosure controls, and making sound decisions in complex cases where new data sources, partner relationships, or high-risk public interest issues require human judgment. As work shifts toward automated data discovery, metadata-driven screening, and reusable processing designs, this capability ensures decisions remain compliant, auditable, and responsible.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 2.5 shifts effort away from manual data discovery and design toward automated source assessment, AI-enabled decision logic, and modular processing with embedded privacy and disclosure controls, leaving staff to resolve the most complex legal, ethical, and partnership issues. This aligns with the change drivers in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which emphasize responsible use of data, modernization through automation and alternative data, and stronger stewardship, transparency, and trust. The current role description does not explicitly cover the advanced legal and ethical judgment now required to validate automated findings and manage partnership risks in this future operating environment.
